L40@P4-6: TABLE OF CONTENTSv
L41@P6: Financing innovation activities is an important challenge
L42@P6: for many firms. Because financial constraints that
L43@P6: reduce investment in innovation hamper long-term
L44@P6: economic growth, policymakers need to understand the
L45@P6: different sources of funding businesses may use to fund
L46@P6: their innovation activities, as well as the interventions
L47@P6: they can develop to provide finance for innovative
L48@P6: businesses.
L49@P6: This paper describes the actors involved and the
L50@P6: types of funding available at different stages of
L51@P6: the innovation process, the rationales for public
L52@P6: intervention, and the advantages and disadvantages of
L53@P6: some of the most commonly used policy instruments.
L54@P6: Innovation activities are more difficult to finance
L55@P6: than other types of investment for several reasons.
L56@P6: Innovation produces an intangible asset that does
L57@P6: not typically constitute accepted collateral to obtain
L58@P6: external funding. Also, the technological and market
L59@P6: uncertainty of innovation activities makes the returns
L60@P6: to investment highly uncertain, creating significant
L61@P6: problems for the standard risk adjustment methods
L62@P6: used by providers of funds.
L63@P6: The importance of each of these conditions in
L64@P6: preventing access to finance for innovative projects
L65@P6: depends on a variety of factors, such as the nature of
L66@P6: the innovation activity and its industry, the size and age
L67@P6: of the firm, and the stage of the innovation process.
L68@P6: This paper uses a streamlined version of an innovation
L69@P6: process with three stages to categorize the different
L70@P6: sources of finance available; in reality, considerable
L71@P6: crossover takes place among instruments because
L72@P6: innovation processes are not discrete.
L73@P6: KNOWLEDGE CREATION AND IDEA
L74@P6: GENERATION
L75@P6: Innovation begins with an idea, sometimes in response
L76@P6: to a particular challenge or to take advantage of a
L77@P6: new opportunity. The amount of resources required
L78@P6: for this first stage of the innovation process varies
L79@P6: widely, depending on the type of innovation being
L80@P6: created.
L81@P6: Raising external finance specifically for the first stage of
L82@P6: the innovation process can be very difficult, since there is
L83@P6: a high level of asymmetric information and no easy ways
L84@P6: to align incentives. Knowledge and ideas are intangible,
L85@P6: uncertainty is typically very high, and spillovers are
L86@P6: thought to be stronger. This is especially the case for
L87@P6: small, young companies with few assets and revenues.
L88@P6: As a result, governments are often among the few
L89@P6: sources of external funding potentially available for
L90@P6: particularly high-risk projects in this stage of the
L91@P6: innovation process. While several forms of public
L92@P6: funding exist, the most common are R&D grants and
L93@P6: R&D tax incentives.
L94@P6: The choice between using grants or tax incentives
L95@P6: to support private investment in innovation involves
L96@P6: several tradeoffs, which explains why the approaches
L97@P6: used by different governments can vary greatly.
L98@P6: Businesses have much to gain by adopting innovations
L99@P6: not developed in house. They can face several barriers
L100@P6: that hamper technology diffusion, however, such as
L101@P6: information asymmetries between producers and users,
L102@P6: high costs of switching to new technologies, high
L103@P6: entry costs (especially in areas with important network
L104@P6: effects), and technological path dependencies. Some of
L105@P6-7: EXECUTIVE SUMMARYvi Financing Business Innovation: A Review of External Sources of Funding for Innovative Businesses and Public Policies To Support Them
L106@P7: these can lead to market failures, which governments
L107@P7: may be able to help address.
L108@P7: Most instruments used for financing technology
L109@P7: diffusion are grants, but they can vary from small
L110@P7: payments—such as vouchers for connecting knowledge
L111@P7: providers to small and medium-sized enterprises
L112@P7: (SMEs)—to large programs to support industry-wide
L113@P7: technology upgrading.
L114@P7: PROTOTYPE DEVELOPMENT AND
L115@P7: MARKET DEMONSTRATION
L116@P7: The second stage of the innovation process involves
L117@P7: getting from an idea to a new product, service, or
L118@P7: process by developing prototypes and testing their
L119@P7: potential for adoption in a real environment, be it with
L120@P7: real customers or real employees.
L121@P7: Several forms of finance provision are available at this
L122@P7: stage. Business angels are one of the main source of
L123@P7: finance, typically in the form of equity or convertible
L124@P7: loans. Early-stage venture capital funds, crowdfunding
L125@P7: platforms, accelerators, and big corporates also play
L126@P7: a role. Specialized knowledge and significant due
L127@P7: diligence activity are required.
L128@P7: The public sector can support the development of private
L129@P7: sources of finance serving this stage, but it also provides
L130@P7: funding directly to companies, giving grants and loans as
L131@P7: well as using pre-commercial procurement schemes.
L132@P7: COMMERCIALIZATION AND
L133@P7: SCALING UP
L134@P7: Once an innovation has been developed and
L135@P7: successfully user tested, the next challenge is to take
L136@P7: it to market, start generating revenue, and scale it
L137@P7: up. Two factors affect the ability to obtain finance for
L138@P7: this particular stage as well as its source: the nature of
L139@P7: the investments to be undertaken and the degree of
L140@P7: uncertainty that prevails.
L141@P7: If risks and rewards are very high, venture capital is
L142@P7: typically the only source available. If risk is low and the
L143@P7: investment required involves mainly the acquisition of
L144@P7: easily redeployable tangible assets, then bank debt is more
L145@P7: appropriate. In addition, firms that are scaling up their
L146@P7: innovations may use several other sources of finance, such
L147@P7: as business angels (if the investments required are relatively
L148@P7: small), factoring and invoice discounting, new emerging
L149@P7: forms of intellectual property (IP)-based asset finance,
L150@P7: project finance (for large-scale investments with relatively
L151@P7: low risk), private equity funds, public markets (initial
L152@P7: public offerings—IPOs—and bonds), and corporates.
L153@P7: Governments also play a role, not only with several forms
L154@P7: of intervention to support private providers of finance,
L155@P7: but often also by directly awarding commercialization
L156@P7: grants or loans to innovative businesses.
L157@P7: WHEN SHOULD GOVERNMENT
L158@P7: INTERVENE?
L159@P7: Markets generally provide less finance for innovation
L160@P7: than is socially desirable, due to the existence of
L161@P7: asymmetric information, externalities, coordination
L162@P7: failures, and institutional failures. These can provide a
L163@P7: rationale for government intervention.
L164@P7: Finance interventions are sometimes also justified as part
L165@P7: of a mission-driven policy. Rather than “fixing” a market or
L166@P7: system failure, a government identifies a goal considered
L167@P7: socially desirable (for example, addressing a social
L168@P7: challenge) and designs a set of instruments to increase
L169@P7: access to finance for innovations aimed at tackling it.
L170@P7: Some of these sources of failure vary in severity along
L171@P7: the stages of the innovation process. For instance,
L172@P7: externalities are typically presumed to be higher earlier
L173@P7: in the process than in later stages, when firms are, in
L174@P7: principle, better able to capture the benefits from their
L175@P7: innovations. Similarly, asymmetric information may be
L176@P7: highest in the earliest stages, when very few concrete
L177@P7: outputs exist to show to the financers, than later on,
L178@P7: when the specifications of an innovative product and its
L179@P7: potential market are more visible.
L180@P7: The size and age of the firm are also important to
L181@P7-8: consider, since a large, established firm can use internal Executive summary vii
L182@P8: resources and its better access to different sources of
L183@P8: external finance to raise funding, which can then be
L184@P8: used to fund its innovation projects. In contrast, market
L185@P8: failures are more severe for young, small firms.
L186@P8: The existence of a market failure is not a sufficient
L187@P8: condition for government intervention. The decision
L188@P8: to intervene needs to weigh both benefits and risks,
L189@P8: since several government failures can make public
L190@P8: intervention impractical or even counterproductive.
L191@P8: In other words, not all market failures are fixable, at
L192@P8: least not at a reasonable cost for society (relative to the
L193@P8: benefits of fixing them).
L194@P8: HOW CAN GOVERNMENTS
L195@P8: INTERVENE?
L196@P8: Governments can use a variety of approaches to
L197@P8: increase the availability of finance for innovative
L198@P8: projects:
L199@P8: • Improving framework conditions and financial
L200@P8: regulation, since maintaining well-functioning
L201@P8: institutions that guarantee property rights, enforcing
L202@P8: contracts, and providing efficient bankruptcy
L203@P8: processes are the most important functions
L204@P8: governments can perform.
L205@P8: • Providing funding to innovative firms, either directly
L206@P8: via grants or government venture capital (VC) funds
L207@P8: or indirectly through financial intermediaries, using,
L208@P8: for instance, a fund-of-funds model, loan guarantee
L209@P8: schemes, or provision of tax credits to early-stage investors.
L210@P8: • Providing an array of services, such as setting up
L211@P8: networks of business angels, running investment
L212@P8: readiness programs for entrepreneurs and investors,
L213@P8: setting up or providing support for accelerators and
L214@P8: incubators, or establishing credit mediation services
L215@P8: Several considerations are important when designing
L216@P8: such interventions.
L217@P8: First, a very good understanding of the incentives
L218@P8: of bureaucrats, politicians, financial intermediaries,
L219@P8: and innovative firms is crucial when designing new
L220@P8: schemes. For instance, credit guarantees can give
L221@P8: banks incentive to be less careful when selecting and
L222@P8: monitoring companies. Similarly, while grants and
L223@P8: government loans allow better targeting than credit
L224@P8: guarantee schemes, short-term political objectives and
L225@P8: lobbying by special interest groups may lead to the
L226@P8: funds being misallocated. Therefore, it is necessary
L227@P8: to develop mechanisms that prevent misalignment of
L228@P8: incentives and target funding toward the appropriate
L229@P8: recipients without being overly complex.
L230@P8: Second, both design and implementation failures are
L231@P8: common. Therefore, it is important to put in place a
L232@P8: monitoring system and a rigorous evaluation strategy
L233@P8: to measure the success or failure of public interventions
L234@P8: and change or discontinue them if necessary.
L235@P8: Third, looking at each type of funding and the policies
L236@P8: to support it in isolation is not sufficient. Governments
L237@P8: need to make sure finance is available for all the stages
L238@P8: of the innovation process, since providing large amounts
L239@P8: to support the initial phase may not translate into faster
L240@P8: economic growth if young innovative firms cannot gain
L241@P8: access to follow-on funding to commercialize their
L242@P8: innovations. (The same principle applies to other stages.)
L243@P8: Fourth, access to finance is only one ingredient required
L244@P8: to develop an innovation ecosystem. It is therefore
L245@P8: important to consider the wider policy mixture, which
L246@P8: includes measures to support the different actors in the
L247@P8: innovation system, as well as the networks that connect
L248@P8: them. Access to finance schemes that are too large
L249@P8: given the level of development of the ecosystem can
L250@P8: be counterproductive, so the timing and magnitude of
L251@P8: the interventions need to be adjusted accordingly. An
L252@P8: integrated approach that considers how the different
L253@P8: interventions are linked to each other and exploits its
L254@P8: synergies is therefore preferable.
L255@P8: Fifth, the measures with the greatest impacts are
L256@P8: not necessarily the most expensive ones, so it is
L257@P8: important to consider a wider range of alternatives.
L258@P8: Providing advice (for example, through investment
L259@P8: readiness programs), increasing information available
L260@P8: (for example, through an IP registry), supporting
L261@P8-9: networks (for example, business angels networks), or viii Financing Business Innovation: A Review of External Sources of Funding for Innovative Businesses and Public Policies To Support Them
L262@P9: improving skills (for example, by providing training for
L263@P9: entrepreneurs and managers) are low-cost interventions
L264@P9: that in some cases may have a better rate of return
L265@P9: than large tax incentive and guarantee programs.
L266@P9: Sixth, governments should design monitoring and
L267@P9: evaluation frameworks to assess the extent to which
L268@P9: the objectives of the interventions are achieved.
L269@P9: Progress toward these measurable objectives can
L270@P9: be monitored through intermediate outcomes and
L271@P9: influenced by flexible interventions. The challenges
L272@P9: of monitoring and evaluation involve (1) identifying
L273@P9: the goals the intervention is designed to achieve, (2)
L274@P9: identifying key indicators that can be used to monitor
L275@P9: progress, (3) setting targets, which quantify the level
L276@P9: of the indicators, and (4) tracking progress to inform
L277@P9: policymakers (Khandker et al. 2009). Finally, the quality
L278@P9: of institutions determines both what sources of finance
L279@P9: are available and how much impact public interventions
L280@P9: will have. For instance, countries with poor institutions
L281@P9: are unlikely to be able to effectively deliver complex
L282@P9: access to finance support schemes, due to the risk
L283@P9: of rent seeking and capture, as well as the lack of
L284@P9: experienced civil servants to administer the schemes.
L285@P9: More importantly, the most effective interventions
L286@P9: governments can undertake to increase innovation
L287@P9: financing are not about creating new support
L288@P9: schemes, but rather improving the overall regulatory
L289@P9: and institutional framework within which innovative
L290@P9: firms and finance providers operate. This includes
L291@P9: issues related to contract enforcement, investor
L292@P9: protection, and bankruptcy regulation. Legal
L293@P9: protection of outside investors is an important
L294@P9: determinant of the development of financial markets.
L295@P9: If laws protect investors and are well enforced,
L296@P9: shareholders and creditors will be willing to finance
L297@P9: firms, and financial markets will be more developed.
L298@P9: Protective laws will encourage investors to pay more
L299@P9: for securities because entrepreneurs will return higher
L300@P9: interest rates and distribute more dividends when
L301@P9: the risk expropriation is reduced. Thus, protection
L302@P9: of investors can increase financial development in
L303@P9: terms of both depth and diversification of financial
L304@P9: instruments, thus allowing more entrepreneurs to
L305@P9: finance innovation with external funds. Finally, IP
L306@P9: rights protection stimulates the creation of innovative
L307@P9: financial instruments that facilitate access to external
L308@P9-10: funding.ix
L309@P10: INTRODUCTION:
L310@P10: THE POLICY ENVIRONMENT FOR
L311@P10: FINANCING INNOVATION
L312@P10: Innovation is the main driver of long-term economic
L313@P10: growth. The accumulation of capital, whether in the
L314@P10: form of physical assets such as plants and equipment
L315@P10: or through better human capital, cannot indefinitely
L316@P10: sustain growth unless new products, services,
L317@P10: processes, and/or business models are developed and
L318@P10: implemented (Solow 1957).
L319@P10: While increasing innovation is a priority for advanced
L320@P10: countries, it also has an important role to play in
L321@P10: developing countries and emerging economies.
L322@P10: Catching up with the countries at the technology
L323@P10: frontier requires not only imitating what they have
L324@P10: done, but adapting it to the particular country
L325@P10: circumstances. Innovation is also required to address
L326@P10: some of the specific, yet very important, challenges
L327@P10: developing countries face. And very often developing
L328@P10: countries, free from the constraints of existing systems
L329@P10: and infrastructure, can skip existing technologies and
L330@P10: develop new, radical innovations (as demonstrated by
L331@P10: leapfrogging examples, from Kenya’s M-Pesa mobile
L332@P10: banking to India’s frugal innovation methods).
L333@P10: Several factors contribute to creating an environment
L334@P10: that enables innovation activity, such as an educated
L335@P10: population and sound institutions. One factor is also
L336@P10: consistently ranked among the top barriers firms face
L337@P10: when they want to innovate: unavailability of finance.
L338@P10: Numerous studies have demonstrated innovation
L339@P10: activities are more difficult to finance than other types
L340@P10: of investment.1
L341@P10:  While some firms can use internal
L342@P10: sources to fund their innovation activities, both
L343@P10: entrepreneurs’ savings and firms’ retained earnings are
L344@P10: limited, so many have no option but to raise funding
L345@P10: from external sources.
L346@P10: The aim of this paper is to summarize the different
L347@P10: external sources of funding businesses can use to fund
L348@P10: their innovation activities and some of the interventions
L349@P10: policymakers have developed to enable greater access
L350@P10: to finance for innovative businesses.2
L351@P10: A STREAMLINED VERSION OF AN
L352@P10: INNOVATION PROCESS
L353@P10: The different sources of finance available can be
L354@P10: categorized in several ways, according to the nature
L355@P10: of the actors that provide it, the characteristics of the
L356@P10: instrument, or the stage of the business that is receiving
L357@P10: the funding. This paper uses a streamlined version of
L358@P10: an innovation process with three stages to frame the
L359@P10: discussion. While innovation processes are not this
L360@P10: discrete, but rather very much continuous and intricate,
L361@P10: considering these stages is useful:
L362@P10: 1.Knowledge creation and idea generation
L363@P10: 2.Prototype development and market demonstration
L364@P10: 3.Commercialization and scaling up/replication
L365@P10: The process does not need to be seen as a linear
L366@P10: one that begins with basic research at an R&D lab
L367@P10: and concludes with the commercialization of a new
L368@P10: product. Ideas for new products may arise not only
L369@P10: from new scientific advances, but from customers as
L370@P10: well. Failed prototypes can lead to new ideas, while
L371@P10: many innovations involve reengineering existing
L372@P10: 1 See Hall and Lerner (2009) for a review.
L373@P10: 2 While innovation happens throughout an economy—in businesses, governments, and nonprofit organizations (and often
L374@P10: emerging at the intersection of these different actors)—the
L375@P10-11: focus of this paper is on finance for innovative businesses.x Financing Business Innovation: A Review of External Sources of Funding for Innovative Businesses and Public Policies To Support Them
L376@P11: processes and business models within organizations,
L377@P11: applying lessons learned in the scaling-up phase.
L378@P11: Therefore, while this basic framework can apply to
L379@P11: different types of innovation, from the development
L380@P11: of new products to the redesign of organizational
L381@P11: structures, the importance of each stage and the

L384@P11: The innovation process used here is viewed from

L393@P11: THE RATIONALES FOR PUBLIC
L394@P11: SECTOR INTERVENTION TO SUPPORT
L395@P11: FINANCE FOR INNOVATION
L396@P11: Markets generally provide less finance for innovation
L397@P11: than is socially desirable, which provides a justification
L398@P11: for government intervention.3 Specifically, markets
L399@P11: underinvest in innovation for several reasons (even if, as
L400@P11: discussed below, the severity of market failures can vary,
L401@P11: depending on the stage of the innovation process):
L402@P11: 1.Asymmetric information: Information about
L403@P11: the likelihood of success of a particular innovation
L404@P11: project is not only limited, but asymmetric. The
L405@P11: entrepreneur (or firm) looking for finance has more
L406@P11: accurate information than potential investors about
L407@P11: how promising an innovation project is, as well as
L408@P11: about the entrepreneur’s effort and choices when
L409@P11: developing it. This leads to two classical sources of
L410@P11: market failure:
L411@P11: a.Adverse selection: If banks don’t know the
L412@P11: default risk of a particular borrower, they can only
L413@P11: price a loan based on the average default risk. As
L414@P11: a result, low-risk borrowers face higher interest
L415@P11: rates than they would if there were perfect
L416@P11: information, and they may choose not to seek
L417@P11: loans. This increases the risk of the remaining
L418@P11: pool of borrowers, since those who are willing to
L419@P11: pay high interest rates are usually also high-risk.
